questions.q: Which standard proteinogenic amino acid contains a guanidinium group on its side chain?
questions.explain: Arginine has a side chain containing a guanidinium group with a high pKa (~12.5), keeping it positively charged at physiological pH. Lysine has an epsilon-amino group, and histidine has an imidazole ring.

open.q: Which standard amino acid features a guanidinium group in its side chain?

questions.q: Which aromatic amino acid contains a phenolic hydroxyl group that can be phosphorylated by protein kinases?
questions.explain: Tyrosine possesses a phenolic -OH group that serves as a site for reversible phosphorylation in cell signaling and is a precursor for catecholamines and thyroid hormones. Phenylalanine lacks this hydroxyl group, and tryptophan has an indole ring.

open.q: Which aromatic amino acid has a phenolic hydroxyl group capable of phosphorylation?

questions.q: Which group consists entirely of branched-chain amino acids?
questions.explain: Isoleucine, leucine, and valine are the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) with aliphatic branched hydrocarbon side chains. They are essential amino acids metabolized primarily in extrahepatic tissues such as skeletal muscle.

open.q: Name the three branched-chain amino acids found in proteins.

questions.q: Which stereochemical configuration predominates in amino acids incorporated into human proteins?
questions.explain: Ribosomes synthesize proteins exclusively using L-alpha-amino acids. D-amino acids occur rarely in nature, such as in certain bacterial cell walls or peptide antibiotics.

open.q: Which stereochemical series do amino acids in human proteins belong to?

questions.q: For a neutral amino acid with ionizable alpha-carboxyl (pKa1 = 2.2) and alpha-amino (pKa2 = 9.4) groups, what is its isoelectric point (pI)?
questions.explain: For a neutral amino acid without an ionizable side chain, pI equals (pKa1 + pKa2) / 2, which is (2.2 + 9.4) / 2 = 5.8. At pH 5.8, the net charge is zero.

open.q: Calculate the isoelectric point of a neutral amino acid with pKa1 of 2.2 and pKa2 of 9.4.

questions.q: When a neutral amino acid is placed in a strongly acidic solution well below its pKa1, what is its predominant ionic form?
options: Cationic form with a net charge of +1
Zwitterionic form with a net charge of 0
Anionic form with a net charge of -1
Uncharged non-ionic form with no protons
questions.explain: At pH well below pKa1, both the carboxyl group (-COOH) and amino group (-NH3+) are protonated, giving a net positive charge of +1. Raising pH above pKa1 deprotonates the carboxyl group to form the zwitterion.

open.q: What is the predominant charge state of a neutral amino acid at a pH much lower than its pKa1?

questions.q: Which chemical reaction joins two amino acids to form a peptide bond?
questions.explain: Formation of an amide (peptide) bond between the alpha-carboxyl group of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of another releases one molecule of water (condensation). Breaking the bond requires addition of water (hydrolysis).

open.q: What type of reaction forms a peptide bond between two amino acids with elimination of water?

questions.q: By convention, in which direction is the primary amino acid sequence of a polypeptide written?
options: From interior disulfide bond to C-terminus
From highest pKa residue to lowest pKa residue
questions.explain: Polypeptide sequences are standardly written starting with the free alpha-amino (N-) terminal residue on the left and ending with the free alpha-carboxyl (C-) terminal residue on the right, matching the direction of translation.

open.q: From which end to which end is a polypeptide primary sequence conventionally written?

questions.q: In a beta-pleated sheet, how do the R-groups of adjacent amino acid residues along a single strand project?
options: Alternating above and below the plane of the sheet
All pointing straight into the central hydrophobic core
All pointing parallel to the hydrogen bonds
Restricted to the interior of a right-handed coil
questions.explain: In a beta-strand, the polypeptide backbone is extended in a zig-zag conformation so successive side chains point alternately above and below the plane of the sheet. This minimizes steric hindrance between adjacent R-groups.

open.q: How are side chains oriented along a single beta-strand in a beta-pleated sheet?
accept: alternating above and below the plane
above and below the sheet plane

questions.q: Which fibrous protein has a triple-helix structure rich in glycine-X-Y repeats, where X is frequently proline and Y is hydroxyproline?
questions.explain: Collagen consists of three intertwined alpha-chains forming a triple helix with repeating Gly-X-Y triplets. Glycine is required every third position because its tiny hydrogen side chain fits inside the crowded central axis of the triple helix.

open.q: Which structural protein forms a triple helix composed of repeating Gly-X-Y motifs?

questions.q: A patient presents with easy bruising, bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and perifollicular hemorrhages after a diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables. Impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis is caused by deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explain: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency, which impairs prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases by failing to keep iron in its reduced ferrous (Fe2+) state. Without adequate hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, collagen triple helices are unstable and cross-linking is defective.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin impairs proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen synthesis, causing scurvy?

questions.q: In a water-soluble globular protein folded in an aqueous environment, where are hydrophobic amino acid side chains typically located?
options: Buried in the interior core away from water
Exposed evenly across the entire outer surface
exclusively at the N-terminal and C-terminal ends
Linked exclusively to surface carbohydrate chains
questions.explain: Globular proteins fold so nonpolar hydrophobic side chains cluster in the interior away from aqueous solvent, while polar and charged side chains generally face outward to interact with water. This arrangement stabilizes tertiary structure via the hydrophobic effect.

open.q: Where are nonpolar amino acid side chains typically positioned in a folded water-soluble globular protein?

questions.q: Which proteins assist newly synthesized polypeptides in folding properly and prevent inappropriate aggregation?
questions.explain: Molecular chaperones (such as Hsp70 and chaperonins like GroEL/Hsp60) bind exposed hydrophobic regions on folding intermediates to guide proper tertiary folding and prevent aggregation. They do not dictate final structure independently of primary sequence.

open.q: Which class of proteins helps nascent polypeptides fold correctly and prevents unwanted aggregation?

questions.q: What is preserved when a globular protein undergoes reversible denaturation by urea or heat?
questions.explain: Denaturation disrupts non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, hydrophobic packing) that maintain secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure, while peptide bonds of the primary structure remain intact. If mild, refolding can restore native structure.

open.q: Which structural feature of a protein remains intact during denaturation?

questions.q: Which class of conjugated proteins contains a non-amino-acid lipid prosthetic group?
questions.explain: Lipoproteins combine a protein component (apoprotein) with lipids such as triacylglycerols, phospholipids, and cholesterol to transport hydrophobic lipids in blood. Glycoproteins contain covalently attached oligosaccharide chains.

open.q: Which class of conjugated proteins consists of protein combined with lipid components?

questions.q: Which oxidation state of iron in the heme prosthetic group is required for reversible oxygen binding in hemoglobin and myoglobin?
questions.explain: Heme binds molecular oxygen reversibly only when its iron atom is in the ferrous (Fe2+) oxidation state. Oxidation to the ferric (Fe3+) state forms methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen.

open.q: In which oxidation state must heme iron be to bind oxygen reversibly in hemoglobin?

questions.q: Why does myoglobin display a hyperbolic oxygen-binding curve rather than the sigmoidal curve of hemoglobin?
options: Myoglobin is monomeric and lacks subunit cooperativity
Myoglobin contains four heme groups per molecule
Myoglobin binds oxygen only in acidic tissues
Myoglobin has lower oxygen affinity than hemoglobin at all pO2 values
questions.explain: Myoglobin is a single-chain (monomeric) protein with one heme group, so oxygen binding shows no cooperative allosteric interaction between subunits, yielding a hyperbolic curve. Hemoglobin is a tetramer exhibiting positive cooperativity (sigmoidal curve).

open.q: Why does myoglobin have a hyperbolic oxygen dissociation curve instead of a sigmoidal one?
accept: single polypeptide chain lacking cooperative binding

questions.q: How does an increase in hydrogen ion concentration (lower pH) in metabolically active tissues affect hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect)?
options: Decreases oxygen affinity to promote oxygen unloading
Increases oxygen affinity to prevent oxygen release
Has no effect on oxygen binding
Converts hemoglobin permanently into fetal hemoglobin
questions.explain: Higher H+ concentration (and higher CO2) protonates specific histidine residues and stabilizes the low-affinity T (tense) state of hemoglobin, lowering oxygen affinity and facilitating oxygen delivery to active tissues.

open.q: How does a decrease in pH (increased H+) alter hemoglobin oxygen affinity during the Bohr effect?

questions.q: A patient exposed to incomplete combustion fumes presents with headache, confusion, cherry-red skin, and normal arterial pO2 on blood gas analysis despite severe cellular hypoxia. Which molecule binds hemoglobin with roughly 200-fold greater affinity than oxygen?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide binds tightly to heme Fe2+ with about 200 times the affinity of oxygen, displacing O2 and shifting the remaining bound O2 curve to the left so tissues cannot extract oxygen effectively. Standard PaO2 measures dissolved O2 and can appear normal.

open.q: Which gas binds hemoglobin with about 200 times the affinity of oxygen, causing functional hypoxia?

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis), what is the primary role of sodium dodecyl sulfate?
options: Denatures proteins and imparts a uniform negative charge proportional to mass
Separates proteins strictly by their native isoelectric point
Cleave peptide bonds at specific basic amino acids
Precipitates proteins selectively using heavy metal ions
questions.explain: SDS binds along polypeptide chains at a roughly constant mass ratio, denaturing them and conferring a uniform negative charge per unit mass so migration through polyacrylamide pores separates primarily by molecular weight.

open.q: What does SDS do to proteins during SDS-PAGE separation?
accept: denatures them and gives a uniform negative charge per mass
linearizes proteins and coats them with negative charge
denatures and imparts uniform negative charge

questions.q: A child develops musty-smelling urine, developmental delay and seizures. Which enzyme deficiency is classically responsible for phenylketonuria?
questions.explain: Classic phenylketonuria most commonly results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing phenylalanine accumulation and reduced tyrosine formation. Some cases result from impaired tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism.

open.q: What is the usual enzyme defect in classic phenylketonuria?

questions.q: A neonate has poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy and a characteristic sweet odour to the urine. Which enzyme complex is most likely deficient?
questions.explain: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, impairing oxidative decarboxylation of leucine-, isoleucine- and valine-derived alpha-ketoacids.

open.q: Which enzyme complex is deficient in maple syrup urine disease?

questions.q: A patient has lens dislocation, a tendency to thrombosis and elevated plasma homocysteine. Which enzyme deficiency is a classic cause?
questions.explain: Classical homocystinuria commonly results from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, impairing conversion of homocysteine and serine to cystathionine. Elevated homocysteine increases thrombotic risk and may cause ectopia lentis and skeletal features.

open.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes classical homocystinuria?

questions.q: Which enzyme incorporates free ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate in the mitochondrial urea cycle?
questions.explain: Mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses free ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate. It is activated by N-acetylglutamate; CPS II is cytosolic and uses glutamine in pyrimidine synthesis.

open.q: Which enzyme incorporates free ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate in the mitochondrial urea cycle?

questions.q: During transamination, the amino group from most amino acids is transferred to which acceptor to form glutamate?
questions.explain: Aminotransferases commonly transfer amino groups to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate and the corresponding alpha-ketoacid. Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) is the coenzyme for these reactions.

open.q: Which ketoacid commonly accepts amino groups during transamination to form glutamate?

questions.q: Which amino acid carries much of the amino nitrogen from skeletal muscle to the liver in the glucose-alanine cycle?
questions.explain: Alanine transports amino nitrogen from skeletal muscle to the liver in the glucose-alanine cycle. In the liver, its amino group can enter nitrogen disposal pathways, while its carbon skeleton is used for gluconeogenesis.

open.q: Which amino acid carries much of the amino nitrogen from skeletal muscle to the liver in the glucose-alanine cycle?

questions.q: A patient has alkaptonuria with darkening urine on standing and ochronosis. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explain: Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase in tyrosine degradation. Homogentisic acid accumulates, oxidises on standing and deposits as pigment in connective tissues, causing ochronosis.

open.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes alkaptonuria?

questions.q: A patient recovering from major surgery is receiving adequate energy and protein. Which state is most consistent with net tissue protein synthesis during recovery?
questions.explain: Positive nitrogen balance occurs when nitrogen intake exceeds nitrogen loss, indicating net retention of nitrogen for tissue growth or repair. It is expected during growth, pregnancy and recovery from catabolic illness when nutrition is adequate.

open.q: Define positive nitrogen balance and give one setting in which it occurs.
accept: Nitrogen intake exceeds nitrogen loss; occurs in growth, pregnancy or tissue repair
Net nitrogen retention during growth or recovery

questions.q: A child with phenylketonuria has developmental delay and musty-smelling urine. Which amino acid becomes conditionally essential?
questions.explain: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. In phenylketonuria, tyrosine can no longer be synthesised adequately from phenylalanine.

open.q: Why does tyrosine become conditionally essential in phenylketonuria?
accept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency prevents adequate conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine

questions.q: A neonate has hyperammonaemia, low blood urea nitrogen and suspected ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Which urinary metabolite is characteristically increased?
questions.explain: Excess mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate enters pyrimidine synthesis, increasing orotic acid excretion. This is a useful clue to ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

open.q: Why is urinary orotic acid increased in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency?
accept: Excess carbamoyl phosphate enters pyrimidine synthesis and increases orotic acid production

questions.q: A patient with vitamin B6 deficiency has impaired activity of several aminotransferases. Which active coenzyme form of vitamin B6 is required for these reactions?
questions.explain: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6, temporarily accepts and transfers amino groups during transamination. Deficiency can impair amino acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

open.q: Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required by aminotransferases?

questions.q: During amino acid catabolism, glutamate undergoes oxidative deamination in mitochondria to release free ammonia. Which enzyme catalyses this reaction?
questions.explain: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyses the reversible oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and NH4+. It is located in the mitochondrial matrix and can use NAD+ or NADP+ as a cofactor.

open.q: Which mitochondrial enzyme catalyses oxidative deamination of glutamate?

questions.q: A methylation reaction in the synthesis of creatine consumes the major activated methyl-group donor formed from methionine and ATP. Which compound donates the methyl group?
questions.explain: Methionine reacts with ATP to form S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), a high-energy methyl-group donor used in numerous methylation reactions, including steps in creatine and epinephrine synthesis. After donating its methyl group, SAM becomes S-adenosylhomocysteine.

open.q: What is the principal activated methyl-group donor derived from methionine?

questions.q: A student is asked to classify tyrosine according to its catabolic products. Which description is correct?
questions.explain: Tyrosine is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Its degradation yields fumarate, which can contribute to gluconeogenesis, and acetoacetate, a ketone-body precursor.

open.q: Is tyrosine glucogenic, ketogenic, or both?

questions.sub: Cysteine and sulfur amino acid metabolism
questions.q: Cysteine can be synthesised from homocysteine through the transsulfuration pathway. Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required by the key enzymes of this pathway?
questions.explain: The transsulfuration pathway converts homocysteine and serine to cystathionine and then cysteine. Cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase require pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6.

open.q: Which vitamin-derived coenzyme is required for the transsulfuration pathway that forms cysteine?

questions.q: A child with a urea-cycle disorder has severe hyperammonaemia due to deficiency of ornithine transcarbamylase. Which reaction is directly impaired?
options: Transfer of the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine to form citrulline
Formation of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate
Cleavage of argininosuccinate to arginine and fumarate
Hydrolysis of arginine to urea and ornithine
questions.explain: Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyses the mitochondrial reaction between ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline. Deficiency causes hyperammonaemia and increased urinary orotic acid.

questions.q: A neonate with maple syrup urine disease has elevated branched-chain amino acids and their corresponding alpha-ketoacids. Which metabolic step is defective?
questions.explain: The branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex catalyses oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoacids derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine. Its deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease.

questions.q: A patient with classical phenylketonuria is placed on a restricted-phenylalanine diet. Why must tyrosine also be supplied?
options: Tyrosine becomes conditionally essential because phenylalanine hydroxylation is impaired
Tyrosine is required to activate phenylalanine hydroxylase
Phenylalanine is normally converted directly into tyrosine by tyrosinase
Tyrosine prevents intestinal absorption of phenylalanine
questions.explain: Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. In classical PKU, impaired conversion means tyrosine must be provided in the diet.

questions.q: A patient with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is being considered for pyridoxine therapy. Why may vitamin B6 help some patients?
options: Pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor for cystathionine beta-synthase
Pyridoxine directly converts homocysteine into methionine
Vitamin B6 replaces the missing enzyme by acting as a structural protein
questions.explain: Cystathionine beta-synthase is a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme. Some variants retain residual activity that can respond to high-dose pyridoxine.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, skeletal muscle releases alanine for hepatic gluconeogenesis. Which reaction in the liver allows alanine's amino group to be transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate?
options: Alanine aminotransferase reaction producing pyruvate and glutamate
Glutamate dehydrogenase reaction producing alanine and ammonia
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I reaction producing alanine
questions.explain: Alanine aminotransferase transfers alanine's amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing pyruvate and glutamate. Pyruvate can enter gluconeogenesis while glutamate carries nitrogen toward urea formation.
